questions.question_text: Six months after the death of her husband, a 70-year-old woman presents with overwhelming sadness, anger regarding her husband\'s unexpected death from a heart attack, intense yearning for him to return, and persistent inability to sort through or dispose of his belongings despite financial necessity. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of major depressive disorder.
A diagnosis of posttraumatic stress disorder.
A diagnosis of prolonged grief disorder (complicated grief).
A major depressive episode cannot be diagnosed within the first 6 months after loss.
A diagnosis of normative stress reaction.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of prolonged grief disorder (complicated grief).

questions.explanation: The clinical features — intense yearning for the deceased, anger about the unexpected death, inability to engage with practical tasks involving the deceased\'s belongings, and significant functional impairment at six months — are the hallmark features of prolonged grief disorder (complicated grief). The Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry (p.155) describes complicated grief as an \'intense and prolonged reaction to bereavement… strong yearnings for the person who has died… disbelief and anger about the death… reminders of the loss are avoided… impairment in work and social functioning.\' DSM-5-TR classifies this as Prolonged Grief Disorder (F43.8); ICD-11 requires a minimum of six months\' duration, which is met here. Adjustment disorder with depressed mood is incorrect because bereavement reactions are explicitly distinguished from adjustment disorder, and the symptom profile is grief-specific rather than a maladaptive response to a general stressor. MDD, while diagnosable in bereavement per DSM-5, does not best capture a presentation dominated by yearning, anger, and avoidance of reminders.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old single woman reports having experienced auditory and persecutory delusions for 2 months, followed by a full major depressive episode with sad mood, anhedonia, and suicidal ideation lasting 3 months. Although the depressive episode resolves with pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy, the psychotic symptoms persist for another month before resolving. What diagnosis best fits this clinical picture?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic, with mixed features
Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

questions.explanation: During this period of illness, the woman’s symptoms concurrently met criteria for a major depressive episode and Criterion A for schizophrenia. Auditory hallucinations and delusions were present both before and after the depressive phase. The duration of the depressive episode was not brief relative to the total duration of the psychotic disturbance, which establishes a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder.

He has insomnia and fatigue, feels guilty, has thoughts he would be better off dead, and has thought about how he could die without anyone knowing it was a suicide. His wife informs you that he requests sex several times a day and that she thinks he may be going to “massage parlors” regularly, both of which are changes from his typical behavior. He has told her he has ideas for a “better Internet,” and he has invested thousands of dollars in software programs that he cannot use. She notes that he complains of fatigue but sleeps only 1 or 2 hours each night and seems to have tremendous energy during the day. Which diagnosis most accurately describes this patient?

options.text: A diagnosis of major depressive episode.
Major depressive episode, with mixed features.
Major depressive episode, with catatonic features.

correct_answer.text: Major depressive episode, with mixed features.

questions.explanation: The specifier “with mixed features” now denotes the coexistence of at least three manic symptoms insufficient to satisfy criteria for a manic epi240 | Depressive Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE sode, within a major depressive episode. This change is based on findings from studies of family history and diagnostic stability showing that the presence of mixed features in an episode of major depressive disorder increases the likelihood that the illness exists in a bipolar spectrum. This likelihood was judged insufficient to assign such individuals a diagnosis of bipolar disorder. The presence of a full manic syndrome within a depressive episode will continue to be an exclusion criterion for a depressive disorder diagnosis, and individuals with this pattern will be considered to have a manic episode.

questions.question_text: Which of the following groups contains diagnoses that were newly introduced or significantly reorganised as standalone categories in the DSM-5 chapter on depressive disorders, compared with DSM-IV?

options.text: Depressive disorder due to another medical condition, medication-induced depressive disorder, and subsyndromal depression.
Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, premenstrual dysphoric disorder
Depressive disorder due to another medical condition, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and substance/medication-induced depressive disorder.
Persistent depressive disorder, medication-induced depressive disorder, and mixed anxiety-depressive disorder.
Substance/medication-induced depressive disorder, persistent depressive disorder, and adjustment disorder with depressed mood.

correct_answer.text: Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, premenstrual dysphoric disorder

questions.explanation: In DSM-5, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder and premenstrual dysphoric disorder are the two diagnoses most unambiguously new to the depressive disorders chapter; DMDD was not a DSM-IV category at all, and PMDD was elevated from a DSM-IV appendix research category to a full diagnosis. Persistent depressive disorder consolidates DSM-IV dysthymia and chronic major depressive disorder and is therefore better described as reorganised than entirely new. Options A, C, D, and E all contain items that either did not change substantially from DSM-IV or include non-existent DSM-5 categories such as subsyndromal depression and mixed anxiety-depressive disorder, making B the best available answer despite its imprecision.

questions.question_text: A 31-year-old woman with no prior diagnosis of mood symptoms reports that she experiences distressing mood lability and irritability starting about 4 days before the onset of menses. She feels “on edge,” cannot concentrate, has little enjoyment from any of her activities, and experiences bloating and swelling of her breasts. The patient reports that these symptoms started 6 months ago when she began taking oral contraceptives for the first time. If she stops the oral contraceptives and her symptoms remit, what would the diagnosis be?

options.text: A diagnosis of premenstrual dysphoric disorder.
A diagnosis of major depressive episode.
A diagnosis of substance/medication-induced depressive disorder.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of substance/medication-induced depressive disorder.

questions.explanation: If the woman stops the hormones and her symptoms disappear, this is consistent with substance/medication-induced depressive disorder. Some women who present with moderate to severe premenstrual symptoms may be using hormonal contraceptives. If such symptoms occur after initiation of exogenous hormone use, the symptoms may be due to the use of hormones rather than the underlying condition of premenstrual dysphoric disorder.

questions.question_text: Which of the following features most clearly distinguishes disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DMDD) from bipolar disorder in children?

options.text: Presence of elevated or expansive mood

questions.explanation: DMDD is distinguished from bipolar disorder primarily by the chronic, non-episodic nature of its irritability. In bipolar disorder, mood disturbance occurs in discrete episodes, whereas in DMDD, irritability is persistent and present between outbursts. Additionally, elevated or expansive mood and grandiosity — hallmark features of mania — are not characteristic of DMDD (DSM-5-TR p.307).

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which features confers a worse prognosis for a patient with bipolar II disorder?

options.text: A diagnosis of higher educational level.

questions.explanation: A rapid-cycling pattern is associated with a poorer prognosis. Return to previous level of social function for individuals with bipolar II disorder is more likely for individuals of younger age and with less severe depression, suggesting adverse effects of prolonged illness on recovery. More education, fewer years of illness, and being married are independently associated with functional recovery in individuals with bipolar disorder, even after diagnostic type (I vs. II), current depressive symptoms, and presence of psychiatric comorbidity are taken into account.

questions.explanation: People with major depression have up to a five-fold increased risk of myocardial infarction. This is one of the significant physical morbidity associations with depression requiring integrated management.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man with a prior diagnosis of a prior depressive episode is given an antidepressant by his family doctor to help with his depressive symptoms. Two weeks later, his doctor contacts you for a consultation because the patient now is euphoric, has increased energy, racing thoughts, psychomotor agitation, poor concentration and attention, pressured speech, and a decreased need to sleep. These symptoms began with the initiation of the patient’s new medication. The patient stopped the medication after 2 days, as he no longer felt depressed; however, the symptoms have continued ever since. What is the patient’s diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of bipolar I disorder.
A diagnosis of bipolar II disorder.
A diagnosis of major depressive disorder.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of bipolar I disorder.

questions.explanation: Manic symptoms or syndromes that are attributable to the physiological effects of a drug of abuse (e.g., in the context of cocaine or amphetamine intoxication), the side effects of medications or treatments (e.g., steroids, L-dopa, antidepressants, stimulants), or another medical condition do not count toward the diagnosis of bipolar I disorder. However, a fully syndromal manic episode that arises during treatment (e.g., with medications, electroconvulsive therapy, light therapy) or drug use and persists beyond the physiological effect of the inducing agent (i.e., after a medication is fully out of the individual’s system or the effects of electroconvulsive therapy would be expected to have dissipated completely) is sufficient evidence for a manic episode diagnosis (Criterion D). The diagnostic features of substance/ medication-induced bipolar and related disorder are essentially the same as those for mania, hypomania, or depression. A key exception to the diagnosis of substance/medication-induced bipolar and related disorder is the case of hypomania or mania that occurs after antidepressant medication use or other treatments and persists beyond the physiological effects of the medication. This condition is considered an indicator of true bipolar disorder, not substance/medication-induced bipolar and related disorder.

questions.explanation: Long-term follow-up studies show a conversion rate from unipolar depression to bipolar disorder (development of mania/hypomania) of approximately 1–2% per year. Over 10 years, at the lower estimate of ~1% per year.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man with two previous episodes of major depression over the past 8 years now presents with a new depressive episode. He achieved partial remission (HAMD = 10) at 3 months of treatment but continues to have residual symptoms despite adequate medication trials. What is his prognosis regarding the next 15 months?
questions.explanation: This patient has two previous episodes (70% recurrence risk within 5 years), partial remission at 3 months (predicts recurrence), AND residual symptoms after treatment (Paykel data: 75% relapse/recurrence risk in 15 months). The 75% figure from Paykel et al. regarding residual symptoms is the most specific predictor in this clinical scenario and exceeds the 70% risk from episode count alone. ---

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is the treatment of choice for premenstrual dysphoric disorder?
questions.explanation: The term premenstrual syndrome (PMS) was fi rst coined by a physician from England named Katharina Dalton in 1953; however, premenstrual tension was a term used prior to this. More than 150 different symptoms have been attributed to PMS, but the one unifying concept is that these symptoms must occur during the (late) luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, causing signifi cant impairment in a woman’s functioning, and must disappear within the fi rst few days of menses. The American Psychiatric Association recognizes premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) as a subset of PMS that was designed to focus on women with severe symptoms causing marked impairment in functioning. PMDD has a lifetime prevalence of approximately 2–4% in menstruating women. Sixty-fi ve per cent of women with unipolar mood disorder experience PMS, and women with PMS have a 60% lifetime prevalence of major depression. In a recent meta-analysis on the effi cacy of SSRIs in PMDD, 15 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were found demonstrating SSRIs as effective for behavioural and physical symptom amelioration and have the best evidence to date. Other supplements do not have solid research evidence to support their use to date, including vitamin E, vitamin A, magnesium, primrose oil, dong quai, black cohosh, wild yam, St John’s wort, or kava. questions.question_text: Children with disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DMDD) often meet criteria for what additional DSM-5 diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of pediatric bipolar disorder.
A diagnosis of oppositional defiant disorder.
A diagnosis of intermittent explosive disorder.
A diagnosis of major depressive disorder.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of oppositional defiant disorder.

questions.explanation: Because chronically irritable children and adolescents typically present with complex histories, the diagnosis of DMDD must be made while considering the presence or absence of multiple other conditions. The differential diagnosis of DMDD from both bipolar disorder and oppositional defiant disorder requires careful consideration. DMDD differs from bipolar disorder in that the former is chronic, whereas the latter is episodic. DMDD differs from oppositional defiant disorder in that very severe irritability is required in the former but not the latter. For this reason, while most children who meet criteria for DMDD will also meet criteria for oppositional defiant disorder, the reverse is not the case.

questions.question_text: Adverse life events are consistently linked to depression. Which ONE of the following statements about this relationship is FALSE?

options.text: 40% of those with depression have no history of preceding significant life events
Suicide attempters have a higher amount of life events than depressed individuals
The frequency of desirable (gain/success) life events in depressed individuals is comparable to that in controls
The impact of life events is moderated by contextual threat, as operationalised in the Life Events and Difficulties Schedule
No reverse causality exists between depression and life events

questions.explanation: Option E is false because reverse causality between depression and life events HAS been demonstrated: Kendler (1997) showed in over 2000 female twins that genetic liability to depression was associated with a significantly increased risk of experiencing stressful life events such as assault, marital problems, and job loss — meaning depression vulnerability can itself cause more life events

He is getting a lot of work done, but recalls a similar episode 10 years ago during which he made imprudent business decisions resulting in marked impairment. A physical examination and laboratory work are unrevealing. He had taken fluoxetine for a depressive episode but self-discontinued it 3 months ago. Which diagnosis best fits this clinical picture?

options.text: Other specified bipolar disorder and related disorder

questions.explanation: This patient most likely meets criteria for bipolar I disorder, current episode hypomanic, which is defined as a current hypomanic episode in an individual with a previous history of at least one manic episode. The history of a past manic episode 10 years ago rules out bipolar II disorder, and the long period since medication discontinuation makes a medication-induced episode unlikely.

questions.question_text: What distinguishes the depressive episodes linked to bipolar II disorder from those linked to bipolar I disorder?

options.text: They are less frequent than those linked to bipolar I disorder.
They are lengthier than those linked to bipolar I disorder.
They are less disabling than those linked to bipolar I disorder.
They are less severe than those linked to bipolar I disorder.
They are most commonly treated with mood stabilizers rather than antidepressants.

correct_answer.text: They are lengthier than those linked to bipolar I disorder.

questions.explanation: The recurrent major depressive episodes associated with bipolar II disorder are typically more frequent and lengthier than those associated with bipolar I disorder. The depressive episodes can be very severe and disabling; because of this, DSM-5 stresses that bipolar II disorder should not be considered a “milder” form of bipolar I disorder. Bipolar II patients are more likely to seek treatment when depressed than during hypomanic episodes.

She denies changes in sleep or appetite, feeling guilty or worthless, or ever having suicidal ideation. Other times, “I’m up and ready to go, and feel like I can be the life of the party. Because there are some manic symptoms, she cannot be diagnosed with a unipolar depressive disorder. questions.question_text: A 9-year-old boy is brought in for evaluation because of explosive outbursts when he is frustrated with schoolwork. The parents report that their son is well behaved and pleasant at other times. Which diagnosis most accurately describes this clinical picture?

options.text: A diagnosis of disruptive mood dysregulation disorder.
A diagnosis of pediatric bipolar disorder.
A diagnosis of intermittent explosive disorder.
A diagnosis of major depressive disorder.
A diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia).

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of intermittent explosive disorder.

questions.explanation: Children with intermittent explosive disorder present with instances of severe temper outbursts much like those in children with disruptive mood dysregulation disorder. However, unlike children with disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, children with intermittent explosive disorder do not exhibit persistent disruption in mood between outbursts. Thus, the two diagnoses are mutually exclusive and cannot be made in the same child. For children with outbursts and intercurrent, persistent irritability, the diagnosis of disruptive mood dysregulation disorder should be made. For children with outbursts but no such irritability, the diagnosis of intermittent explosive disorder should be made.

questions.question_text: According to large epidemiological studies such as the STAR*D dataset, which of the following symptoms is most commonly reported by patients with a major depressive episode?
questions.explanation: Insomnia and sleep disturbance are consistently identified as the most commonly reported symptoms in patients with major depression across large epidemiological studies, including STAR*D and WHO collaborative data, affecting approximately 70–80% of patients. While decreased energy (Option B) is also very prevalent, it does not consistently rank above sleep difficulties in prevalence data. Poor appetite, poor concentration, and suicidal ideation are all genuine symptoms of depression but are less frequently reported than sleep disturbance or fatigue. Option E (suicidal ideation) is among the least prevalent symptoms statistically.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old female is brought to your outpatient clinic by her friend, who reports that she has been acting differently for the past 4 days. The friend describes elevated mood and increased energy. On interview, the patient reports sleeping no more than 3 hours per night but feeling great. Her speech is pressured and her thoughts are racing. She denies any previous episodes of elevated or depressed mood and reports a family history of major depressive disorder. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of bipolar I disorder
Bipolar II disorder, with rapid cycling
Other specified bipolar and related disorder

correct_answer.text: Bipolar II disorder, with rapid cycling

questions.explanation: This patient presents with a 4-day episode of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and racing thoughts, which meets the minimum duration for hypomania (four or more days) but not mania (seven or more days required for Bipolar I). She has no prior depressive episode, which precludes Bipolar II disorder (which requires both hypomanic and depressive episodes per Kaplan and Sadock Synopsis p.795). Rapid cycling requires four or more mood episodes within 12 months and cannot be assigned on the basis of a single first episode (Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines 2025, p.339). Because the presentation does not meet full criteria for any specific bipolar disorder category, Other specified bipolar and related disorder (DSM-5-TR F31.89, p.1216) is the most appropriate diagnosis.

questions.question_text: A 42-year-old woman with major depression and comorbid anxiety has shown good response to treatment (50% symptom reduction). However, she continues to meet criteria for anxiety disorder independently. According to NICE guidelines, which next management step is most appropriate?

options.text: Increase antidepressant dose to target anxiety
Continue antidepressant; anxiety often improves as depression improves
Add a second-line antidepressant specifically for anxiety
Refer for hospitalization due to comorbidity

correct_answer.text: Continue antidepressant; anxiety often improves as depression improves

questions.question_text: Which statement incorrectly describes how grief differs from a major depressive episode (MDE)?

options.text: In grief, the individual typically focuses on the lost person; in MDE, thoughts center on personal failures.
Humor and positive affect in grief are always pathological signs of complicated grief.
The thought content linked to grief generally features a preoccupation with thoughts and memories of the deceased, rather than the self-critical or pessimistic ruminations seen in MDE.
In grief, feelings of worthlessness and self-loathing are common; in MDE, self-esteem is generally preserved.

If a bereaved patients thinks about death and dying, such thoughts are generally focused on the deceased and possibly about “joining” the deceased, whereas in MDE such thoughts are focused on ending one’s own life because of feeling worthless, undeserving of life, or unable to cope with the pain of depression.

correct_answer.text: In grief, feelings of worthlessness and self-loathing are common; in MDE, self-esteem is generally preserved.

questions.explanation: In distinguishing grief from an MDE, it is useful to consider that in grief the predominant affect is feelings of emptiness and loss, while in MDE it is persistent depressed mood and the inability to anticipate happiness or pleasure. The dysphoria in grief is likely to decrease in intensity over days to weeks and occurs in waves, the so-called pangs of grief. These waves tend to be associated with thoughts or reminders of the deceased. The depressed mood of MDE is more persistent and not tied to specific thoughts or preoccupations. The pain of grief may be accompanied by positive emotions and humor that are uncharacteristic of the pervasive unhappiness and misery characteristic of MDE. The thought content associated with grief generally features a preoccupation with thoughts and memories of the deceased, rather than the self-critical or pessimistic ruminations seen in MDE. In grief, selfesteem is generally preserved, whereas in MDE feelings of worthlessness and self-loathing are common. If self-derogatory ideation is present in grief, it typically involves perceived failings vis-à-vis the deceased (e.g., not visiting frequently enough, not telling the deceased how much he or she was loved). If a bereaved individual thinks about death and dying, such thoughts are generally focused on the deceased and possibly about “joining” the deceased, whereas in MDE such thoughts are focused on ending one’s own life because of feeling worthless, undeserving of life, or unable to cope with the pain of depression.

These symptoms may be accompanied by behavioral and physical symptoms. Symptoms must have occurred in most of the menstrual cycles during the past year and must have an adverse effect on work or social functioning. Typically, symptoms peak around the time of the onset of menses. While the core symptoms include mood and anxiety symptoms, behavioral and somatic symptoms commonly also occur. In order to confirm a provisional diagnosis, daily prospective symptom ratings are required for at least two symptomatic cycles.

The lack of any current hypomanic symptoms rules out a mixed episode of the illness. The presence of major depressive episodes rules out cyclothymic disorder, and this patient’s hypomanic episodes rule out major depressive disorder. This vignette is illustrative of the clinical observation that patients with bipolar II disorder generally present for treatment only when they experience depressive symptoms.

He recalls how at the time it seemed “like I could do anything.” During that time he was glad to feel rested after 3 hours of sleep and recalls looking into becoming a CEO. His friends told him that he needed to slow down. Two weeks after this very enjoyable period, his enthusiasm “crashed,” leaving him depressed. He was treated with fluoxetine in the past, but it caused him to become restless, anxious, and irritable, so he stopped taking it. With this further information, the individual’s most likely psychiatric diagnosis is:

options.text: A diagnosis of major depressive disorder
Bipolar I disorder, current episode depressed
Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic with mixed features
Bipolar II disorder, current episode depressed

correct_answer.text: Bipolar I disorder, current episode depressed

questions.explanation: When a patient presents with a major depressive episode, it is necessary to inquire about previous manic or hypomanic symptoms because a major depressive episode may occur as part of bipolar disorder. Bipolar I disorder is a chronic, recurrent mood disorder characterized by the presence of at least one manic episode and usually recurrent major depressive episodes. A manic episode is a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood lasting at least 1 week, or any duration if hospitalization is necessary. During the mood episode, symptoms such as grandiosity, inflated selfesteem, flight of ideas, goaldirected hyperactivity, pressured speech, excessive involvement in pleasurable activities, and marked impairment in occupational, social, and relationship functioning are prominent. Another key feature during a manic episode is the decrease need for sleep. Bipolar II disorder is also a chronic disorder that requires at least one hypomanic and one major depressive episode but is commonly marked by severe, recurrent, often psychotic depression. Cyclothymic disorder is characterized by a 2year period during which there have been numerous periods of hypomanic symptoms that do not meet criteria for a hypomanic or manic episode and numerous periods of depressive symptoms that do not meet criteria for a major depressive episode. The current or most recent episode should be specified when diagnosing bipolar disorder.

questions.question_text: A 26-year-old man presents with his first depressive episode currently lasting 8 weeks. He is requesting information about prognosis and when he might expect symptom resolution. Based on epidemiological data, what is the most accurate counselling point?

options.text: Most episodes resolve spontaneously within 2 weeks
Untreated episodes typically last 6–13 months; treated episodes last about 3 months
Complete recovery occurs in fewer than 15% of first episodes
Without treatment, his symptoms will persist permanently
First episodes always remit by 12 weeks regardless of treatment

correct_answer.text: Untreated episodes typically last 6–13 months; treated episodes last about 3 months

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that untreated depressive episodes last 6 to 13 months, while most treated episodes last about 3 months. His 8-week untreated illness is within the natural duration window. The median duration is 12 weeks, so he can be counselled that treatment could shorten this to approximately 3 months, providing realistic expectations and reinforcing treatment engagement. --- **END OF 40 MCQs** --- ## Summary Statistics: **Difficulty Distribution:** - **Easy (1-Step, 40%):** Questions 1–4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 13, 18, 22, 25, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34 (14 questions) - **Medium (2-Step, 30%):** Questions 5, 7, 10, 11, 14, 15, 17, 19, 20, 21, 27, 28, 29, 35, 39 (11 questions) - **Difficult (3-Step, 30%):** Questions 16, 23, 24, 26, 36, 37, 38, 40 (8 questions, with 24, 26, 36, 37, 38, 40 requiring differential analysis) **Stem Type Distribution:** - **Fact-Focus (60%):** Questions 1–24, 28–32 (25 questions) - **Case Vignette (10%):** Questions 37–40 (4 questions) - **Incomplete Statements (30%):** Questions 25–27, 33–36 (9 questions)

questions.question_text: An irritable 8-year-old child has a prior diagnosis of temper outbursts both at home and at school. What characteristic mood feature must be also present to qualify him for a diagnosis of disruptive mood dysregulation disorder?

options.text: The child’s mood between outbursts is generally euthymic.
The child’s mood between outbursts is generally hypomanic.
The child’s mood between outbursts is generally depressed.
The child’s mood between outbursts is generally irritable or angry.
The symptoms must have occurred for at least 1 year without remission to qualify.

correct_answer.text: The child’s mood between outbursts is generally irritable or angry.

questions.explanation: Criterion D of disruptive mood dysregulation disorder requires that the child’s mood between temper outbursts be persistently irritable or angry most of the day, nearly every day, and observable by others (e.g., parents, teachers, peers).

questions.question_text: What would be the greatest predisposing factor for suicide attempts in bipolar disorder?
questions.explanation: The most consistently demonstrated risk factor for suicide in bipolar disorder is prior suicide attempt. Suicide rates are high among patients with bipolar spectrum illness. The lifetime prevalence for suicide occurs in an estimated 10% to 15% of individuals with bipolar I disorder.

questions.question_text: Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) is a popular concept but not formally considered as a separate category under current classifi catory systems. Which of the following statements is true with regard to this condition?

options.text: Seasonal depression carries lower familial risk of affective disorders than non-seasonal depression
In phototherapy for SAD, exposure to skin is equally effective as exposure to eye
Early-morning light treatment is more effective than evening exposure
Side-effects of exposure are more intense with evening than morning treatment
Conventional antidepressants are less effective on seasonal depression than summer depression

correct_answer.text: Early-morning light treatment is more effective than evening exposure

questions.explanation: ICD-10 clinical guidelines do not include specifi c criteria for SAD. However, specifi c criteria are included in DSM-IV (Text Revision) and the research version of ICD-10. ICD-10 provisional criteria for SAD specifi es the disorder as a subtype of mood disorder where three or more episodes must occur with onset within the same 90-day period of the year for three or more consecutive years; Remissions also occur within a particular 90-day period of the year. Seasonal episodes must outnumber any non-seasonal episodes that may occur. Familial risks of affective disorders in SAD are similar to those found in non-seasonal depressive illnesses. Typical depressive symptoms of SAD respond better to bright-light therapy whereas atypical symptoms respond to phototherapy at all intensities. In phototherapy retinal light exposure is important; skin absorption is not suffi cient to modify circadian rhythms or depressive symptoms. Early-morning phototherapy is superior but leads to more side-effects, such as easy startle, gastrointestinal intolerance and headaches. Conventional antidepressants have also been reported to have a therapeutic effect in SAD. Stein G and Wilkinson G, eds. Seminars in General Adult Psychiatry, 2nd edn. Gaskell, 2007, p. 13. Rodin I and Thompson C. Seasonal affective disorder. Advances in Psychiatric Treatment, 1997; 3: 352–359.

questions.question_text: A individual exhibits atypical depression, including increased sleep, increased appetite with weight gain, mood reactivity, and rejection sensitivity. Which of the following attributes of her presentation is most likely to persist throughout life?
questions.explanation: Pathological sensitivity to perceived interpersonal rejection is a feature of atypical depression that has an early onset and persists, occurring during periods of depression and euthymia. It may be exacerbated during depressive episodes. The other features of atypical depression (mood reactivity, increased appetite, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis) are more likely to resolve with appropriate treatment. Re FeRe NCe McInnis, M. G., Riba, M., & Greden, J. F. (2014). Depressive disorders. In R. E. Hales, S. C. Yudofsky, & L. W. Roberts (Eds.), The American Psychiatric Publishing textbook of psychiatry (6th ed.). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which features of a depressive episode may be more suggestive of bipolar disorder rather than a recurrent major depressive disorder?

options.text: Marked anxiety and agitation as opposed to psychomotor retardation
Poor acute antidepressant response to lithium

questions.explanation: Characteristics of a depressive episode occurring as a part of bipolar disorder includes a history of hypomania, onset in the teens, an equal sex ratio, more common postpartum onset, more common acute onset, with higher likelihood of psychomotor retardation as opposed to agitation and anxiety. Further, lithium produces an acute antidepressant effect in bipolar depression that might be absent in unipolar depression.

questions.question_text: A 39-year-old woman reports that she became quite depressed in the winter last year when her company closed for the season, but she felt completely normal in the spring. She recalls experiencing several other episodes of depression over the past 5 years (for which she cannot identify a seasonal pattern) that would have met criteria for major depressive disorder. which of the following options correctly summarizes this patient’s eligibility for a diagnosis of “major depressive disorder, with seasonal pattern”?

options.text: She qualifies only if she has documentation of seasonal episodes from prior years.
She qualifies because her symptoms are specific to winter and will likely improve in spring.
She does not qualify for this diagnosis: the patient must have had two episodes with a seasonal relationship in the past 2 years and no nonseasonal episodes during that period.
She does not qualify because the symptoms are linked to an identifiable psychosocial stressor.
She qualifies because the episode began in November and the symptoms meet criteria for MDE.

correct_answer.text: She does not qualify for this diagnosis: the patient must have had two episodes with a seasonal relationship in the past 2 years and no nonseasonal episodes during that period.

questions.explanation: The “with seasonal pattern” specifier requires a regular temporal relationship between the onset of major depressive episodes (MDEs) in major depressive disorder or in bipolar I or bipolar II disorder and a particular time of the year (e.g., in the fall or winter). The diagnosis excludes cases in which there is an obvious effect of seasonal-related psychosocial stressors (e.g., regularly being unemployed every winter). Full remissions (or a change from major depression to mania or hypomania) also occur at a characteristic time of the year (e.g., depression disappears in the spring). In the past 2 years, two MDEs must have occurred that demonstrate the temporal seasonal relationships defined above, and no nonseasonal MDEs must have occurred during that same period. Seasonal MDEs must substantially outnumber the nonseasonal MDEs that may have occurred over the individual's lifetime. The specifier “with seasonal pattern” can be applied to the pattern of MDEs in bipolar I disorder, bipolar II disorder, or major depressive disorder, recurrent.

questions.question_text: Which of the following features is associated with a good prophylactic response to lithium in bipolar disorder?

options.text: Presence of family history of Psychosis
Good antimanic effi cacy during acute episode

questions.explanation: Complete inter-episode recovery (euthymia between episodes) is one of the most robustly cited predictors of good prophylactic response to lithium in bipolar disorder. Other recognised predictors include a family history of lithium response in a first-degree relative, a mania-depression-euthymia (MDI) sequence, and fewer prior episodes. Absence of neurological signs is not a primary predictor. Good acute antimanic response to lithium has some predictive value but is less consistently cited as a primary prophylactic predictor than inter-episode recovery.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man with major depression achieved full remission after 16 weeks of treatment (HAMD score <7). He had symptoms for 8 months before treatment initiation. According to the Kupfer Curve definitions in the source, if he maintains this remission state continuously for 9 months from the end of acute treatment, what is his clinical status?

options.text: In remission but not yet recovered

questions.explanation: Recovery as achieving remission and continuing even after the natural period of an untreated depressive episode (usually >6m after the acute period). At 9 months post-acute treatment, he has exceeded the 6-month threshold while maintaining remission, thus meeting the definition of recovered status. His initial 8-month untreated episode duration supports that >6 months applies to his case. ---

questions.question_text: What percentage of those who sought help for depression in the EseMED study were given drug therapy?
questions.explanation: According to DEPRES data (related to EseMED findings), only 31% of those who sought help were given drug therapy, and among these, only 25% were given antidepressant drugs specifically. This indicates that even among those accessing care, pharmacological treatment is underutilized. ---

questions.question_text: A 32-year-old man reports 1 week of feeling unusually irritable. During this time, he has increased energy and activity, sleeps less, and finds it difficult to sit still. He also is more talkative than usual and is easily distractible, to the point of finding it difficult to complete his work assignments. A physical examination and laboratory workup are negative for any medical cause of his symptoms and he takes no medications. What diagnosis most accurately describes this clinical picture?

options.text: Major depressive episode with psychomotor agitation.
A diagnosis of major depressive episode.

questions.explanation: In DSM-5, the definition of a manic episode has been broadened to include both an abnormal mood (elevated, expansive, or irritable) and increased activity for at least 1 week. The person must also experience at least three (four if the mood is irritable) of the following symptoms: 1) inflated selfesteem or grandiosity, 2) decreased need for sleep, 3) more talkative than usual or pressure to keep talking, 4) flight of ideas or subjective experience that thoughts are racing, 5) distractibility, 6) increase in goal-directed activity or psychomotor agitation, and 7) excessive involvement in activities that have a high potential for painful consequences.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman with newly diagnosed bipolar disorder attends an outpatient appointment to discuss long-term management. Which intervention is an essential component of bipolar disorder treatment?
questions.explanation: Psychoeducation about illness, triggers, early warning signs is essential in bipolar management.

questions.question_text: According to the epidemiological data in the source, a 32-year-old woman with depression has recently developed her first hypomanic episode. Which of the following factors would most support a diagnosis of bipolar II rather than representing treatment-related hypomania?
questions.explanation: The source lists Factors associated with a change of polarity from unipolar to bipolar as including younger age, family history of bipolarity, antidepressant-induced hypomania, hypersomnia and retarded phenomenology. A family history of bipolarity suggests an inherent bipolar diathesis rather than treatment-induced mood elevation. Options B, D, and E all can be associated with antidepressant-induced hypomania. Female sex actually shows bipolar onset often with depression. ---

questions.question_text: Adverse life events are consistently linked to depression. Which of the following statements with respect to the above relationship is NOT true?

options.text: 40% of those with depression have no history of preceding significant life events
Suicide attempters have a higher amount of life events than depressed individuals
Gain or success events are not more frequent in depressed individuals compared to non-depressed controls
The Life Events and Difficulties Schedule rates the impact of life events according to their contextual threat to the individual
No reverse causality exists between depression and life events

correct_answer.text: No reverse causality exists between depression and life events

questions.explanation: Option E is false because Kendler (1997) explicitly demonstrated reverse causality: genetic vulnerability to depression was associated with a significantly increased risk of experiencing stressful life events, meaning depression (or its liability) can itself increase exposure to life events. This has been directly demonstrated in a sample of over 2000 female twins.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man returns to the mental health center after having been prescribed a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) for the past 6 weeks. He states that he is now able to focus much better in his law school classes. His mood has improved to the point that he does not “feel like there’s always a dark cloud over my head.” He reports increased energy, which he attributes to getting 7 hours of sleep a night “for the first time in years,” and to “finally being hungry enough to eat as much as everyone else.” He ends by saying “I thought everyone felt the same way I did. I didn’t realize I could feel good most of the time. I had just felt so bad for so long.” What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Though this patient is reporting being happy, it is in the context of not feeling as sad, as opposed to grandiosity. There is no history of mania, so bipolar disorder and cyclothymia would not be diagnosed... He reports feeling depressed almost all of the time, which is more consistent with persistent depressive disorder than major depressive disorder, which has discrete episodes.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which sleep changes is seen in individuals with depression?

options.text: A diagnosis of dependent personality disorder
A diagnosis of paranoid personality disorder
A diagnosis of avoidant personality disorder
A diagnosis of paranoid personality disorder

questions.explanation: Pica, previously categorized as a “disorder of infancy or early childhood,” has been recategorized as a “feeding and eating disorder” in DSM5 because the disorder can begin at any age, although childhood onset is most common. A diagnosis of pica requires that the patient be eating nonnutritive, nonfood substances for at least 1 month and that this is not accounted for by the patient’s developmental level. It is also important to rule out this type of behavior as being socially acceptable within the patient’s culture. Rumination disorder involves the regurgitation of food following meals, and anorexia nervosa requires a low body weight as part of its criteria. ARFID, which is new in DSM5, is characterized by restriction of food intake as in anorexia, but patients with ARFID do not have fear of gaining weight or misperceptions about body image as seen in anorexia. Although pica may be seen in patients with intellectual disability, this patient has no history of developmental delay.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old woman reports that during every menstrual cycle she experiences breast swelling, bloating, hypersomnia, an increased craving for sweets, poor concentration, and a feeling that she cannot handle her normal responsibilities. She notes that she also feels somewhat more sensitive emotionally and may become tearful when hearing a sad story. She takes no oral medication but does use a drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol patch. What diagnosis most accurately describes this clinical picture?

options.text: A diagnosis of premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).
A diagnosis of substance/medication-induced depressive disorder.

questions.explanation: Premenstrual syndrome differs from PMDD in that a minimum of five symptoms is not required and there is no stipulation of affective symptoms for individuals who suffer from premenstrual syndrome. This condition may be more common than PMDD, although the estimated prevalence of premenstrual syndrome varies. Premenstrual syndrome shares with PMDD the feature of symptom expression during the premenstrual phase of the menstrual cycle, but it is generally considered to be less severe than PMDD. Individuals who experience physical or behavioral symptoms in the premenstruum, without the required affective symptoms, likely meet criteria for premenstrual syndrome and not for PMDD.

The patient has no prior prior diagnosis of a mood disorder, and all of the depressive symptoms are temporally related to the hypothyroidism. Based on this information, you determine that a change in diagnosis—to depressive disorder due to another medical condition—is warranted, as well as a specifier to indicate that full criteria for MDD are not met. How would the full diagnosis be recorded?
