questions.explanation: In recording a diagnosis of depressive disorder due to another medical condition, the name of the other medical condition is inserted in the mental disorder diagnosis (i.e., “depressive disorder due to hypothyroidism”). In addition, the other medical condition should be coded and listed separately immediately before the depressive disorder due to the medical condition. In this vignette, the full coding would be “244.9 [E03.9] hypothyroidism; 293.83 [F06.31] depressive disorder due to hypothyroidism, with depressive fea256 | Depressive Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE tures.” (The “with depressive features” specifier denotes that full criteria are not met for a major depressive episode.) There is no longer an Axis III in DSM-5.

questions.question_text: Which diagnostic category accounts for the largest proportion of diagnostic changes among patients initially diagnosed with depression?
questions.explanation: In longitudinal studies of diagnostic stability, bipolar disorder is the most frequently identified re-diagnosis among patients initially diagnosed with depression, reflecting the common clinical scenario of unrecognised hypomania or mania emerging over time. Neurotic/stress-related disorders, personality disorders, and schizophrenic spectrum disorders account for a smaller proportion of diagnostic conversions from depression. Adjustment disorders would typically be diagnosed instead of depression, not as a subsequent conversion from it.

questions.question_text: The most powerful predictors of relapse of depressive episodes among the following is

options.text: Previous episodes of depression and presence of residual symptoms
Bipolar diagnosis and earlier age of onset
Male gender and later age of onset
Lower degree of life events and absence of family history
Female gender and past history of hospital admission

correct_answer.text: Previous episodes of depression and presence of residual symptoms

questions.explanation: Follow-up studies in depression reveal two powerful predictors of recurrence: the presence of residual symptoms after apparent recovery and history of previous episodes of depression. The presence of residual symptoms increases the risk of recurrence nearly threefold, whereas past history of depression doubles the risk, with each new episode increasing the risk further. Other possible risk predictors for recurrence include somatic syndrome, reversed vegetative signs, early age of onset, and family history of mood disorders. Recurrence risk is higher in bipolar than in unipolar mood disorders. Stein G and Wilkinson G, eds. Seminars in General Adult Psychiatry, 2nd edn. Gaskell, 2007, p. 17.

questions.question_text: Which factor indicates poor prognosis in depression?

options.text: Sound social functioning for 5 years preceding illness

questions.explanation: The source lists Remission status at 3 months – partial remission predicts recurrence as a relapse indicator. Partial rather than complete remission at this critical timepoint predicts poor long-term outcome. All other options (A, B, D, E) are listed as good prognostic indicators. ---

questions.question_text: A 25yearold female patient reports that for the last several years her mood “never seems to be stable,” and this has been impacting her work and relationships negatively. On further interview she endorses periods of feeling elevated and irritable and other times of feeling abnormally sad, but never so much in either direction to feel “out of control.” When she is irritable, she often has racing thoughts, and her friends sometimes tell her she is speaking too quickly. When she feels low, she cries more often and feels a sense of worthlessness, but she denies any neurovegetative symptoms or suicidal thoughts. She cannot remember the last time she “felt normal” for more than 2 or 3 weeks in a row. Which of the following is the MOST likely diagnosis?

options.text: Chronic major depressive disorder with atypical features
Bipolar II disorder with rapid cycling
A diagnosis of unspecified bipolar disorder

questions.explanation: The following are diagnostic criteria for a diagnosis of cyclothymic disorder: 2 or more years of numerous periods of hypomanic symptoms and periods of depressive symptoms that do not meet criteria for a major mood episode; and symptoms were present for at least half the time, and no period without symptoms was longer than 2 months Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed.). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which populations is MOST at risk for developing a secondary mood disorder (i.e., either substance induced or due to another medical condition)?
questions.explanation: The three most atrisk populations for developing a secondary mood disorder are patients with mixed features, patients with frequent episodes, and the elderly. In geriatric populations this is especially important to keep in mind so as to rule out likely medical or organic causes when a newonset mood disorder is suspected. Re FeRe NCe Ketter, T. A., & Chang, K. D. (2014). Bipolar and related disorders. In R. E. Hales, S. C. Yudofsky, & L. W. Roberts (Eds.), The American Psychiatric Publishing textbook of psychiatry (6th ed.). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man with a history of a prior depressive episode is given an antidepressant. Two weeks later, he is euphoric, has racing thoughts, psychomotor agitation, pressured speech, and a decreased need to sleep. He stopped the medication after 2 days, as he no longer felt depressed; however, the euphoric symptoms have continued fully syndromal for the past two weeks since discontinuation. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A fully syndromal manic episode that arises during treatment and persists beyond the physiological effect of the inducing agent is sufficient evidence for a manic episode diagnosis, leading to a Bipolar I diagnosis. This condition is considered an indicator of true bipolar disorder, not substance/medication-induced bipolar and related disorder.

questions.question_text: What is the 1-year prevalence of depression in the general population?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly notes The 1-year prevalence of depression in the general population was 5.3% while lifetime prevalence was 13%. The 3.3% figure was a point prevalence estimate in 1992, and 7% was the estimate by 2002, but 5.3% is specifically the 1-year prevalence. ---

questions.question_text: According to NESARC data, what is the mean age of onset for major depressive disorder?
questions.explanation: NESARC explicitly states the mean age of onset of depression is 30 years. Approximately 50% of first depressive episodes occur before age 40. While some patients present earlier (aged 25) or later (aged 35+), the epidemiological mean across the population is 30 years. ---

questions.question_text: In which scenario among the following ways do manic episodes differ from attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)?

options.text: Manic episodes are more strongly linked to poor judgment.
Manic episodes are more frequently observed to involve excessive activity.
Manic episodes have clearer symptomatic onsets and offsets.
Manic episodes are more frequently observed to show a chronic course.
Manic episodes occur continuously throughout childhood, while ADHD typically emerges in adolescence.

correct_answer.text: Manic episodes have clearer symptomatic onsets and offsets.

questions.explanation: ADHD and manic episodes are both characterized by poor judgment, excessive activity, impulsive behavior, and denial of problems. Patients with ADHD have an earlier onset of illness (i.e., before age 7 years), show a more chronic course (manic episodes are more episodic), and lack clear onsets and offsets of symptoms. In addition, ADHD patients tend not to have an unusually elevated mood or psychotic symptoms.

questions.question_text: For an adolescent who exhibits distractibility, which of the following additional features would suggest an association with bipolar II disorder rather than attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)?

options.text: A need for less sleep that remains constant throughout the day.
A diagnosis of complaints of racing thoughts.
Evidence that the symptoms are episodic.
Evidence that the symptoms represent the patients’s baseline behavior.

correct_answer.text: Evidence that the symptoms are episodic.

questions.explanation: ADHD may be misdiagnosed as bipolar II disorder, especially in adolescents and children. Many symptoms of ADHD, such as rapid speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, and less need for sleep, overlap with the symptoms of hypomania. The double counting of symptoms toward both ADHD and bipolar II disorder can be avoided if the clinician clarifies whether the symptoms represent a distinct episode and if the noticeable increase over baseline required for the diagnosis of bipolar II disorder is present.

questions.question_text: A 29-year-old woman complains of sad mood every month in anticipation of her very painful menses. The pain begins with the start of her flow and continues for several days. She does not experience pain during other times of the month. She has tried a variety of treatments, none of which have given her relief. What is the appropriate diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of premenstrual dysphoric disorder.
A diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia).

questions.explanation: Dysmenorrhea is a syndrome of painful menses, but this is distinct from a syndrome characterized by affective changes. Symptoms of dysmenorrhea begin with the onset of menses, whereas symptoms of premenstrual dysphoric disorder, by definition, begin before the onset of menses, even if they linger into the first few days of menses.

questions.question_text: Among hospitalised depressed patients followed up for a decade, what is the annual conversion rate to bipolar I disorder?
questions.explanation: That among hospitalised depressed patients followed up for nearly a decade, 1% per year converted to bipolar I and 0.5% per year converted to bipolar II. In community samples, only 1 in 10 develop mania within 10 years. ---

questions.question_text: Which response criterion is defined as a 26–49% decrease in symptom severity compared with baseline?
questions.explanation: That 26–49% decrease in symptom severity compared with baseline is termed partial response. In contrast, achieving 50% symptom-free is termed response, and HAMD < 7 with persistence defines remission. ---

questions.question_text: Comorbidity between PMDD and mood disorders occurs in what proportion of affected women?
questions.explanation: Comorbidity with a mood disorder is seen in 30–70%. This substantial comorbidity rate is clinically significant. Options A, B, D, and E all misrepresent this range. ---

questions.question_text: A qualifier for depressive disorders in DSM5 is “with anxious distress.” Which of the following symptoms does NOT support this diagnosis?

options.text: Fear that something awful will happen

questions.explanation: Symptoms consistent with the specifier “with anxious distress” include feeling keyed up or tense, feeling unusually restless, fear that something awful will happen, difficulty concentrating because of worry, and the feeling that the individual might lose control of himor herself. Loss of appetite may be seen in depressive disorders but is not included in the criteria for this specifier. Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed.). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman reports 2 years of persistently depressed mood, accompanied by loss of pleasure, ruminations of being better off dead, feelings of guilt, and inability to make decisions. She experiences an increased need for sleep but still feels fatigued, and has gained 12 kg. She has never been treated for depression but wonders if she should be hospitalized. Her medical workup is normal. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder, with melancholic features
Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia), with persistent major depressive episode

correct_answer.text: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia), with persistent major depressive episode

questions.explanation: If the major depressive episode has persisted for at least a 2-year duration and remains present, then the specifier “with persistent major depressive episode” is used alongside the persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) diagnosis.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man with classic features of schizophrenia has always experienced co-occurring symptoms of depression—encompassing feeling “down in the dumps,” having a poor appetite, feeling hopeless, and suffering from insomnia—during his episodes of active psychosis. These depressive symptoms occurred only during his psychotic episodes and only during the 2-year period when the patient was experiencing active symptoms of schizophrenia. After his psychotic episodes were successfully controlled by medication, no further symptoms of depression were present. The patient has never met full criteria for major depressive disorder at any time. What is the appropriate DSM-5 diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia).
Bipolar I disorder and persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia).
Depressive disorder due to another medical condition.

questions.explanation: Depressive symptoms are a common associated feature of chronic psychotic disorders (e.g., schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, delusional disorder). A separate diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder is not made if the symptoms occur only during the course of the psychotic disorder (including residual phases).

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old man presenting with a single depressive episode meets criteria for mild depression. According to the source, what approach to management is advocated?

options.text: Watchful waiting with review in 2 weeks if agreed

correct_answer.text: Watchful waiting with review in 2 weeks if agreed

questions.explanation: The NICE guidelines state Watchful waiting with no active intervention for mild depression is an advocated strategy if agreeable; the review must be in 2 weeks. Option A is incorrect because Antidepressants have a poor risk-benefit ratio for mild depression. ---

questions.question_text: A 42-year-old woman with recurrent major depression has just completed acute-phase treatment and achieved full remission. According to the Kupfer Curve conceptual framework, recovery (as distinct from remission) is defined as sustained remission that outlasts which of the following time periods?

options.text: The natural duration of an untreated depressive episode (typically 3–6 months after the acute period)

questions.explanation: According to the Kupfer Curve as described, a patient is in \\\'remission\\\' once no clinically meaningful depressive symptoms are detectable following the treated acute episode. \\\'Recovery\\\' is declared when this remission persists beyond the natural duration of an untreated depressive episode — typically 3–6 months after the acute phase.

questions.question_text: What distinguishes patients with substance/medication-induced depressive disorder from patients with major depressive disorder who do not have a substance use disorder?

options.text: They are more commonly identified as female.
They are more frequently reported to have graduate school education.
They are more commonly identified as male.
They are more commonly identified as white.
They are less frequently observed to report suicidal thoughts/attempts.

correct_answer.text: They are more commonly identified as male.

questions.explanation: In a representative U.S. adult population, compared with individuals with major depressive disorder who did not have a substance use disorder, individuals with substance-induced depressive disorder were more likely to be male, to be black, to have at most a high school diploma, to lack insurance, and to have lower family income. They were also more likely to report higher family history of substance use disorders and antisocial behavior, higher 12-month history of stressful life events, a greater number of DSM-IV major depressive disorder criteria, and feelings of worthlessness, insomnia/ hypersomnia, and thoughts of death and suicide attempts.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman reports 2 years of persistently depressed mood, accompanied by loss of pleasure in all activities, ruminations that she would be better off dead, feelings of guilt about “bad things” she has done, and thoughts about quitting work because of her inability to make decisions. Although she has never been treated for depression, she feels so distressed at times that she wonders if she should be hospitalized. She experiences an increased need for sleep but still feels fatigued during the day. Her overeating has led to a 12-kg weight gain. She denies drug or alcohol use, and her medical workup is completely normal, encompassing laboratory tests for vitamins. The consultation was prompted by her worsened mood for the past several weeks. What is the most suitable diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of major depressive disorder (MDD).
Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia), with persistent major depressive episode.
A diagnosis of bipolar II disorder.
A diagnosis of mDD, with melancholic features.

correct_answer.text: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia), with persistent major depressive episode.

questions.explanation: The essential feature of persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) is a depressed mood that occurs for most of the day, for more days than not, for at least 2 years. This disorder represents a consolidation of DSM-IVdefined chronic major depressive disorder and dysthymic disorder. Major depression may precede persistent depressive disorder, and major depressive episodes may occur during persistent depressive disorder. Individuals whose symptoms meet major depressive disorder criteria for 2 years should be given a diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder as well as major depressive disorder. If there is a depressed mood plus two or more symptoms meeting criteria for a persistent depressive episode for 2 years or more, then the diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder is made. The diagnosis depends on the 2-year duration, which distinguishes it from episodes of depression that do not last 2years. If the symptom criteria are sufficient for a diagnosis of a major depressive episode at any time during this period, then the diagnosis of major depression should be noted, but it is coded not as a separate diagnosis but rather as a specifier with the diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder. If the individual’s symptoms currently meet full criteria for a major depressive episode, then the specifier “with intermittent major depressive episodes, with current episode” would be applied. If—as in the patient described in the above vignette—the major depressive episode has persisted for at least a 2-year duration and remains present, then the specifier “with persistent major depressive episode” is used. When full major depressive episode criteria are not currently met but there has been at least one previous episode of major depression in the Depressive Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE | 251 context of at least 2 years of persistent depressive symptoms, then the specifier “with intermittent major depressive episodes, without current episode” is used. If the individual has not experienced an episode of major depression in the past 2 years, then the specifier “with pure dysthymic syndrome” is used.

questions.question_text: The 1-year prevalence of dysthymia is estimated to be around
questions.explanation: Dysthymia has a 1-year prevalence of 1–3%. The lifetime prevalence according to the National Comorbidity Survey 1994 is 6%. Dysthymia has a high comorbidity with other psychiatric disorders, particularly major depression. In one series, only about 25–30% of cases were observed to occur over a lifetime in the absence of other psychiatric disorders. The comorbidity of personality disorders seems to be very high (60–80%). Early-onset dysthymia is defi ned as having onset before age 21. Stein G and Wilkinson G, eds. Seminars in General Adult Psychiatry, 2nd edn. Gaskell, 2007, p. 14.

questions.question_text: Which personality disorder cluster, with one exception, shows strong associations with lifetime major depressive disorder?
questions.explanation: That Cluster C personality disorders, except anankastic (obsessive-compulsive) PD, show strong associations with lifetime MDD. Cluster A disorders are typically associated with psychotic spectrum conditions, and Cluster B with impulsivity and mood instability but not depression specifically. ---

questions.question_text: According to NICE guidelines, when depression and anxiety are comorbid, which condition should be treated first?
questions.explanation: NICE guidelines specify that if comorbid depression and anxiety are present, treat the depression first. This sequential approach reflects the evidence that treating the primary depression often improves secondary anxiety symptoms. ---

questions.question_text: Over a lifetime, how many times more episodes do bipolar patients experience compared to unipolar depressives?
questions.explanation: Over a lifetime, bipolar patients experience twice as many episodes as unipolar depressives. This reflects the more chronic and episodic nature of bipolar disorder compared to unipolar depression. ---

questions.question_text: What is the minimum duration of depressed mood required to diagnose persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) in adults?
questions.explanation: The essential feature of persistent depressive disorder is a depressed mood that occurs for most of the day, for more days than not, for at least 2 years in adults (or at least 1 year for children and adolescents).

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old graduate student complains of feeling down and “not enjoying anything” for the past month, along with insomnia and poor appetite. She recalls a similar episode 1 year ago. She also reports several episodes of increased energy in the past 2 years lasting 1–2 weeks, during which she sleeps less but feels energetic, very productive, and more outgoing. Friends note she speaks more rapidly during these times but find her clever, and she exhibits no marked functional impairment during these high-energy periods. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder, current episode depressed
Bipolar I disorder, current episode unspecified
Bipolar II disorder, current episode depressed

correct_answer.text: Bipolar II disorder, current episode depressed

questions.explanation: Because her periods of mood elevation do not cause distress or impairment, they are probably hypomanic episodes, hence a diagnosis of bipolar II disorder. The presence of major depressive episodes rules out cyclothymic disorder, and this patient’s hypomanic episodes rule out major depressive disorder.

questions.question_text: According to Kaplan and Sadock\'s Synopsis of Psychiatry, which of the following best describes the prognostic role of comorbid psychiatric disorders in major depressive disorder?

options.text: They are associated with better outcomes
They are poor prognostic indicators associated with worse outcomes
They have no effect on prognosis
They only affect prognosis in patients with psychotic features

correct_answer.text: They are associated with better outcomes

questions.explanation: Kaplan and Sadock\'s Synopsis of Psychiatry (p.816) explicitly lists \'the absence of a comorbid psychiatric disorder and of a personality disorder\' among the additional good prognostic signs in major depressive disorder, meaning their presence predicts worse outcomes. Options A and B directly contradict this evidence.

questions.question_text: In community studies, approximately what proportion of patients beginning with a depressive episode develop mania within 10 years?
questions.explanation: That in community studies, one in ten patients (10%) who begin with a depressive episode go on to develop an episode of mania within 10 years. This rate increases to nearly 50% in severely depressed hospitalised patients, highlighting the importance of inpatient status as a risk factor. ---

questions.question_text: What is the mean age at which polarity switches from unipolar to bipolar disorder?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states the mean age at which the switch from unipolar to bipolar occurs is 32 years. The average number of previous episodes in those who switch varies between two and four. ---

questions.question_text: What is the average duration of an untreated single major depressive episode?
questions.explanation: The average duration of an untreated single major depressive episode is approximately 6 months (24 weeks).

questions.question_text: Approximately what percentage of individuals who experience a single manic episode will go on to have recurrent mood episodes?
questions.explanation: Bipolar disorders are highly recurrent, and more than 90% of individuals who have a single manic episode go on to have recurrent mood episodes.

questions.question_text: In addition to affective and behavioral symptoms, prospective daily ratings are required to make a diagnosis of premenstrual dysphoric disorder. For how many consecutive symptomatic menstrual cycles is the prospective rating required?
questions.explanation: DSM5 requires confirmation of at least two cycles of prospective daily ratings to make a diagnosis of premenstrual dysphoric disorder. Otherwise, the diagnosis should be accompanied by a “provisional” suffix. Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed.). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

questions.question_text: A patient with a prior diagnosis of bipolar disorder reports experiencing 1 week of elevated and expansive mood. Evidence of which of the following would suggest that the patient is experiencing a hypomanic, rather than manic, episode?

options.text: A diagnosis of decreased need for sleep.
A diagnosis of increased productivity at work.
Impaired insight and denial of problems.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of increased productivity at work.

questions.explanation: The primary factor that differentiates manic and hypomanic episodes is that manic episodes cause marked impairment in social or occupational functioning or necessitate hospitalization to prevent harm to self or others, or there are psychotic features (Criterion C of bipolar I disorder). In hypomania, “The episode is not severe enough to cause marked impairment in social or occupational functioning or to necessitate hospitalization” (Criterion E of bipolar II disorder). Both types of episodes can cause irritability or decreased need for sleep. Insight is not included in the diagnostic criteria.

questions.question_text: A 52-year-old man with major depression has achieved partial remission at 3 months of treatment. According to the prognostic indicators in the source, what is the clinical significance of this finding?
questions.explanation: The source lists Remission status at 3 months – partial remission predicts recurrence as a relapse indicator (negative prognostic factor). This is contrasted with the good prognostic indicator of achieving full remission. Partial remission at this timepoint is a red flag for future relapse risk. ---

questions.question_text: Among those who received drug therapy in the DEPRES study, what percentage were actually prescribed antidepressants?
questions.explanation: Of the 31% who received drug therapy, only 25% were given antidepressant drugs. This means approximately 8% of all those seeking help received appropriate antidepressant pharmacotherapy, highlighting significant gaps in evidence-based prescribing. ---

questions.question_text: According to NICE guidelines, which management approach is advocated for mild depression if the patient agrees?

options.text: Watchful waiting with no active intervention

correct_answer.text: Watchful waiting with no active intervention

questions.explanation: NICE guidelines advocate watchful waiting with no active intervention for mild depression if agreeable, with review in 2 weeks. The source also notes that antidepressants have a poor risk-benefit ratio for mild depression, supporting a conservative initial approach. ---

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which factors is most predictive of incomplete recovery between mood episodes in bipolar I disorder?

options.text: Having a family prior diagnosis of bipolar disorder.
Having a mood episode accompanied by mood-incongruent psychotic symptoms.

correct_answer.text: Having a mood episode accompanied by mood-incongruent psychotic symptoms.

questions.explanation: Incomplete interepisode recovery in bipolar I disorder is more common when the current episode is accompanied by mood-incongruent psychotic features. Being separated, divorced, or widowed and having a family history of bipolar disorder are risk factors for bipolar I disorder; however, they are not predictors of course. Bipolar I disorder is more common in high-income than in low-income countries (1.4% vs. 0.7%), but higher income does not predict incomplete interepisode recovery.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which statements is accurate with regard to the clinical progression of bipolar disorder?

options.text: The duration of mood episodes increases progressively
Initial episodes have slower onset than later episodes
The interval between episodes decreases progressively
Seasonal pattern is more commonly in bipolar type 1 than type 2
Later episodes are less likely to be triggered by life events than the initial episodes

correct_answer.text: The interval between episodes decreases progressively

questions.explanation: In any patient with bipolar disorder, the duration of individual mood episodes tends to be relatively stable throughout the course, with mania generally lasting for a shorter time than depression. But the onset may become more rapid with age. The interval from one episode to the next tends to decrease through the course of illness, although some evidence suggests a tendency for the inter-episode intervals to stabilize after approximately fi ve episodes. Patients with seasonal patterns are more commonly of bipolar II subtype than bipolar I. The fi rst episode is more likely to be triggered by life events than later episodes. Ambelas confirmed the strong correlation between stressful life events and first manic admissions; this association weakens as the illness progresses. This is particularly true for younger bipolar patients with mania rather than depression. This is consistent with the hypothesis of kindling phenomenon in bipolar disorders. Stein G and Wilkinson G, eds. Seminars in General Adult Psychiatry, 2nd edn. Gaskell, 2007, p. 27–29. Ambelas A. Life events and mania: a special relationship? British Journal of Psychiatry 1987; 150: 235–240.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man presents with persistently depressed mood for several weeks that interferes with his ability to work. He has insomnia, fatigue, feels guilty, and has suicidal thoughts. However, his wife notes that he requests sex several times a day, is investing thousands of dollars in software he cannot use, sleeps only 1 or 2 hours each night, and seems to have tremendous energy during the day. Which diagnosis best fits this patient?

options.text: Major depressive episode, with atypical features
Major depressive episode, with melancholic features
Major depressive episode, with mixed features

correct_answer.text: Major depressive episode, with mixed features

questions.explanation: The specifier “with mixed features” now denotes the coexistence of at least three manic symptoms insufficient to satisfy criteria for a manic episode, within a major depressive episode. The presence of a full manic syndrome within a depressive episode will continue to be an exclusion criterion for a depressive disorder diagnosis, but here the patient's primary presentation is a major depressive episode mixed with manic symptoms.

questions.question_text: The Paykel study cited in the source compared relapse rates at 15 months in patients treated to full remission versus those with residual symptoms. What is the approximate difference in relapse risk?
questions.explanation: The risk of relapse or recurrence is significantly higher in patients with residual symptoms (75% in 15 months) after treatment compared with patients who were treated to full remission (25% in 15 months). The difference is 75% minus 25% = 50 percentage points, indicating that treatment to full remission dramatically reduces relapse risk. ---

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman presents with her first depressive episode. She has a strong family history of bipolar disorder, and during her current depression, she reports hypersomnia and psychomotor retardation. What is her greatest risk regarding future diagnosis?

options.text: Persistent dysthymia without other mood episodes
Development of anxiety disorder as comorbidity
Conversion from unipolar to bipolar disorder

correct_answer.text: Conversion from unipolar to bipolar disorder

questions.explanation: This patient has multiple documented risk factors for polarity switch: younger age (28), family history of bipolarity, hypersomnia, and retarded phenomenology (psychomotor retardation). The mean switch occurs at age 32 with 2–4 previous episodes, making bipolar conversion a significant risk rather than permanent unipolar depression or other diagnostic conversions. ---

questions.question_text: Children with disruptive mood dysregulation disorder are most likely to develop which of the following disorders in adulthood?

options.text: A diagnosis of bipolar I disorder.
A diagnosis of bipolar II disorder.
A diagnosis of borderline personality disorder.
A diagnosis of unipolar depressive disorders.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of unipolar depressive disorders.

questions.explanation: Approximately half of children with severe, chronic irritability will have a presentation that continues to meet criteria for the condition 1year later. Rates of conversion from severe, nonepisodic irritability to bipolar disorder are very low. Instead, children with chronic irritability are at risk to develop unipolar depressive and/or anxiety disorders in adulthood.

questions.question_text: A depressed patient reports that he experiences no pleasure from his normally enjoyable activities. which of the following options additional symptoms would be necessary for this patient to qualify for a diagnosis of major depressive disorder with melancholic features?

options.text: Anhedonia, psychomotor agitation, and decreased appetite.
Anhedonia, guilt, and early morning awakening.
Inappropriate guilt, depression that is worse in the morning, and earlymorning awakening.
Psychomotor retardation, insomnia, and decreased concentration.
Anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, and concentration difficulties.

correct_answer.text: Inappropriate guilt, depression that is worse in the morning, and earlymorning awakening.

questions.explanation: Two criteria must be met to qualify for the specifier “with melancholic features” for major depressive disorder. Criterion A specifies that one of the following must be present during the most severe period of the current episode: 1) loss of pleasure in all, or almost all, activities; 2) lack of reactivity to usually pleasurable stimuli (does not feel much better, even temporarily, when something good happens). Criterion B specifies that three (or more) of the following must be present: 1) a distinct quality of depressed mood characterized by profound despondency, despair, and/or moroseness or by so-called empty mood; 2) depression that is regularly worse in the morning; 3) early-morning awakening (i.e., at least 2 hours before usual awakening); 4) marked psychomotor agitation or retardation; 5) significant anorexia or weight loss; 6) excessive or inappropriate guilt. The specifier “with melancholic features” can be applied to the current (or, if the full criteria are not currently met for major depressive episode, to the most recent) major depressive episode in major depressive disorder or in bipolar I or II disorder only if it is the most recent type of mood episode.

questions.question_text: What is the approximate mean duration of an adequately treated major depressive episode?
questions.explanation: The mean duration of a treated (pharmacologically managed) major depressive episode is approximately 3 months. In contrast, untreated depressive episodes typically last around 6 months on average. Stahl\'s 5th edition describes an acute treatment phase of 6–12 weeks, broadly consistent with a ~3-month treated episode duration. Options A (2 months) and D/E (9–12 months) fall outside the standard taught range, and C (6 months) reflects the untreated, not treated, episode duration.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is more common in men with bipolar I disorder than in women with the disorder?
questions.explanation: Although bipolar I disorder affects men and women equally, hypomanic, mixed-state, and rapid-cycling symptoms are more common in women. Alcohol abuse is higher in men than in women in all cases, although it should be noted that women with bipolar disorder have a higher rate of alcohol abuse than do women in the general population. Compared with bipolar men, bipolar women are more likely to experience rapid cycling and anxiety and have higher rates of lifetime comorbid eating disorders.

questions.question_text: How many times greater is the lifetime risk of suicide in individuals with bipolar disorder than in the general population?
questions.explanation: The estimated lifetime suicide risk is 15 times greater for individuals with bipolar disorder than for the general SoRdeRS • 209 population, and bipolar disorder may account for up to 25% of all completed suicides. Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed.). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

questions.question_text: According to epidemiological studies, approximately what percentage of patients with major depressive disorder will make at least one suicide attempt during their lifetime?
questions.explanation: Epidemiological studies suggest that approximately 10–15% of patients with major depressive disorder make at least one suicide attempt during their lifetime. Option C (15%) most closely approximates this classically Option B (9%) corresponds to the general population lifetime prevalence of suicidal ideation across 17 countries (WMH survey data), not the MDD-specific attempt rate.

questions.question_text: According to EseMED European data, what percentage of identified depressed patients received antidepressants in a year?
questions.explanation: EseMED data shows that only 21% of depressed patients received antidepressants in a year, despite one-third consulting their general practitioner and 21% seeing a psychiatrist. This indicates a significant treatment gap between need and treatment provision. ---

questions.question_text: What is the most common symptom reported by patients with depression?
questions.explanation: The most common complaint of patients with depression is reduced energy (97%). About 80% report difficulty sleeping. Eighty-four percent report poor concentration.

questions.question_text: For a patient who has experienced two major depressive episodes, what is the probability of recurrence?
questions.explanation: For those who have had 2 major depressive episodes, the probability of recurrence goes up to 70%. This increases further to 80-95% after three episodes, showing escalating risk with episode number. ---

questions.question_text: Which physical symptom distinguishes PMDD from major depressive disorder?
questions.explanation: That while many of its symptoms overlap with a depressive episode, the physical symptoms of breast pain and bloating are not seen in major depressive disorder. This specific distinction makes option C correct. Options A, B, D, and E are all common to both conditions. ---

questions.question_text: A patient with a prior diagnosis of bipolar I disorder exhibits a new-onset manic episode and is successfully treated with medication adjustment. He notes chronic depressive symptoms that, on reflection, long preceded his manic episodes. He describes these symptoms as “feeling down,” having decreased energy, and more often than not having no motivation. He denies other depressive symptoms but feels that these alone have been sufficient to negatively affect his marriage. Which diagnosis most accurately describes this clinical presentation? Bipolar and Related Disorders—QUESTIONS | 35

options.text: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) with depressive episodes.
Bipolar I disorder and persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia).
A diagnosis of bipolar II disorder.

correct_answer.text: Bipolar I disorder and persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia).

questions.explanation: This patient’s presentation does not meet the full criteria for a major depressive episode and thus would not qualify for a diagnosis of bipolar I disorder, current or most recent episode depressed. If the patient meets criteria for persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) and bipolar I disorder, both should be diagnosed. The presence of a manic episode makes bipolar II disorder, cyclothymic disorder, and other specified bipolar and related disorder inappropriate.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is accurate regarding treatment of premenstrual dysphoric disorder?

options.text: Cyclic discontinuation of sertraline results in significant adverse effects.
Clinical response is seen within 4 to 6 weeks of initiation of sertraline.
Evidence does not support the use of continuous administration of sertraline through the menstrual cycle.
Intermittent dosing of sertraline during the luteal phase has similar efficacy to continuous administration through the menstrual cycle.
Ideal dosing of sertraline for premenstrual dysphoric disorder is 200 mg daily.

correct_answer.text: Intermittent dosing of sertraline during the luteal phase has similar efficacy to continuous administration through the menstrual cycle.

questions.explanation: Intermittent administration and continuous administration of sertraline for treatment of premenstrual dysphoric disorder have similar efficacy. There are no significant adverse effects from cyclic discontinuation. Clinical response is observed within a few days. Sertraline doses of 50 to 150 mg daily are efficacious for treatment of this disorder. Re FeRe NCe Halbreich, U., & Kahn, L. S. (2003). Treatment of premenstrual dysphoric disorder with luteal phase dosing of sertraline. Expert Opinion on Pharmacotherapy, 4, 2065– 2078.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which symptoms is not a diagnostic requirement of the “mixed features” qualifier for a manic or hypomanic episode?
questions.explanation: Atypical depression is a specifier defined by DSM5 including criteria of mood reactivity (mood brightens in response to actual or potential positive events) and two (or more) of the following symptoms: weight gain or increased appetite, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis, and interpersonal rejection sensitivity. MAOIs (Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors) (e.g., phenelzine) are useful in treating atypical depression. Re FeRe NCe Niciu, M. J., Sinclair, C. M., Zarate, C. A., & Shelton, R. C. (2014). Pharmacological and somatic treatments for major depressive disorder. In G. O. Gabbard (Ed.), Gabbard’s treatments of psychiatric disorders (5th ed.). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.
